text: Lesson 21 covered planning a deployment well enough that it shouldn't go wrong. This lesson covers what happens when, despite that planning, it does. There are exactly two real strategies: revert, which restores the exact prior state, and roll forward, which leaves the deployment in place and ships a targeted fix. Neither is automatically right — it depends on what actually broke.

A revert is only as clean as the tooling behind it. The Application Repository's version history restores a scoped application to a previous, known-good version. A specific Update Set or a prior Source Control commit can undo exactly the change that caused the problem. Done cleanly, a revert is powerful because it restores a state the team already knows worked — no guesswork about whether the fix is correct.

Rolling forward means the deployment stays live, and the team ships a small, targeted fix for the specific broken piece instead of undoing everything. This is the right call when the root cause is already understood, the fix is small and low-risk, and reverting would mean giving up other, unrelated functionality from the same deployment that's actually working fine.

Three real questions drive the decision. How severe and widespread is the issue — a cosmetic bug, or a broken critical workflow affecting everyone? Has the root cause of a roll-forward fix actually been identified, and can it realistically be tested quickly? And critically: how clean would the revert actually be?

A messy, overly broad deployment that welds unrelated changes together can be genuinely harder to cleanly revert than to simply fix forward, because reverting it risks undoing other things that are working correctly. How a deployment was batched in the first place shapes how cleanly it can be undone later.

Severity, roll-forward readiness, revert cleanliness — the answers, not a fixed rule, decide revert versus roll forward. Next: a real deployment that goes wrong, walked end to end through this exact decision.
